strengths: The paper gives a broad and coherent study of online fair division under several information regimes (no information, normalization, frequency predictions, identical valuations), covering EF/EFX/EF1/PROP1/MMS and their approximations.

Theorem 5.1 is a strong and elegant meta-algorithm: any feasible share in the single-shot setting can be achieved online with frequency predictions. This yields, for example, the best-known MMS approximation for any n and EFX for n=2, and it generalizes several prior results.

The paper provides matching or tight impossibility results in several regimes, especially the tight (sqrt(5)-1)/2-EFX bound for two agents with identical valuations and normalization information (Theorem 6.3).
It corrects a flawed prior impossibility example (Kahana and Hazon) and strengthens the known EF1 impossibility to rule out any positive approximation factor without information.
The theoretical nature makes reproducibility primarily a matter of proof correctness; the main constructions and reductions are mostly self-contained and checkable.
weaknesses: Algorithm 1 is not well-defined as written. The inactivity test in Lines 7-9 includes the current good and can set all agents inactive before Line 12, leaving arg max over an empty set. The check N' = empty is only performed at the start of the loop, so the pseudocode does not specify what happens when the active set becomes empty mid-iteration. This affects the central positive results in Theorems 4.1 and 4.2.

The proofs of Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 do not explicitly handle the case where N' becomes empty before all goods have arrived. Although the invariant may be salvageable by allocating the current/remaining goods to agent 1, the manuscript does not prove that this preserves EF1/PROP1 for the already-inactive agents.

The proof of Theorem 5.5 contains garbled or incorrect inequalities. For example, it derives a chain v1(B1) > v1(A1') > v1(A2') > v1(B2), contradicting the earlier assumption v1(A1') < v1(A2'), and the substitution step from v1(B2) > v1(A1') to v1(A2') > v1(B2) appears erroneous. The result may be correct, but the presented proof is not convincing as written.

There is a significant inconsistency about PROP1: the abstract and introduction claim that no online algorithm can achieve PROP1 even for two agents, but Section 3 states that the approximation lower bound for PROP1 remains open and only discusses the non-existence of a PROP1 allocation. This overclaims relative to the actual results.

Theorem 3.3 appears to be misstated: 'there is no online algorithm with max envy in Omega(sqrt(T))' is not the usual lower-bound formulation (which would be that every online algorithm has max envy Omega(sqrt(T)), or no o(sqrt(T)) guarantee).

There are several minor technical and presentation errors: e.g., in Theorem 4.1, 'v2(g') >= v2(g')' should involve v1; in Theorem 4.4, a limit is written as delta -> 0 where delta -> infinity is intended; and several citations/names are misspelled.

Some results are incremental over prior work (e.g., the normalization algorithm generalizes Zhou et al., and the identical-valuation results are close to semi-online scheduling), though the frequency-prediction meta-algorithm is genuinely novel.

The paper does not discuss robustness of the frequency-prediction guarantees to noisy or imperfect predictions, which is a natural and important concern in learning-augmented settings; it is only mentioned as future work.

strengths: The paper provides a comprehensive study of online fair division under different information regimes, including no information, normalization information, and frequency predictions, as well as the special case of identical valuations.
The introduction of frequency predictions and the meta-algorithm for share-based fairness notions is a novel and potentially impactful contribution, bridging offline guarantees with online settings.
The algorithm for two agents under identical valuations and normalization information achieves a tight bound for EFX, which is a technically interesting result.
The paper is well-structured and generally clear in its presentation, with a good overview of related work and motivations from online scheduling and learning-augmented algorithms.
weaknesses: There is a significant error in the proof of Theorem 5.6: the limit is taken as $\delta \to 0$ while $\delta$ is defined as a large constant ($\delta > 1$), which undermines the validity of the impossibility result for EFX with frequency predictions for $n \geq 3$.
Several results, such as the PROP1 guarantee for $n \geq 2$ under normalization, are relatively straightforward extensions of prior work and may not constitute a substantial advance.

The frequency prediction model assumes precise knowledge of the multiset of future valuations and the exact number of items, which is a strong assumption; the paper acknowledges but does not address robustness to noisy predictions, limiting practical applicability.
The paper leaves open important questions, such as whether EF1 is achievable for $n \geq 3$ with frequency predictions, and the impossibility for PROP1 without information (only shown for EF1).
Some proofs are overly terse or contain notation inconsistencies (e.g., in Theorem 5.6, the use of $\delta$ in limits and the definition of $V_i$), which hinder reproducibility and clarity.

strengths: Provides a comprehensive and timely study of online fair division under different information structures, including no information, normalization, frequency predictions, and identical valuations.
The general meta-algorithm (Theorem 5.1) showing that any feasible share achievable offline can be achieved online with frequency predictions is elegant, powerful, and likely to be widely applicable.
The tight bound for identical valuations with normalization (Theorem 6.3) is a clean and interesting result, and the accompanying impossibility results are strong.
The new algorithm for normalized valuations (Algorithm 1) achieves EF1 and 0.5-MMS for two agents and PROP1 for any number of agents, improving over prior work.
The paper is well-motivated, connects to semi-online scheduling and learning-augmented algorithms, and raises several interesting open problems.
weaknesses: The proof of Proposition 3.1 contains a gap: in Case 1, the agent who receives no goods may still satisfy EF1 because removing g2 from another agent's bundle leaves zero value for that agent (as the table assigns value 0 to goods g3..g_{n+1} for agents 3..n). The intended table likely should assign positive values to those goods to make the pigeonhole argument valid.

There are several presentation issues and typos: e.g., a garbled sentence in the proof of Theorem 5.5 ('we get that Thus,'), misspelled author names in the references (e.g., 'Allowah' instead of 'Allouah'), and unclear tie-breaking description in the leximin++ proof.

The meta-algorithm (Algorithm 2) requires solving an offline fair-division instance at each arrival. The paper does not discuss the computational complexity of this approach, which may be prohibitive for large instances.

The frequency prediction model assumes exact knowledge of the multiset of future valuations, which is a strong assumption. Robustness to prediction errors is only mentioned as future work, not analyzed.

The paper leaves several natural questions open (e.g., PROP1 approximation without information, EF1 with frequency predictions for n>=3), which is acceptable but limits the completeness of the contribution.

strengths: Comprehensive study of online fair division under three information models (no information, normalization information, frequency predictions), with matching positive algorithms and impossibility results.
Algorithm 1 provides a new and non-trivial guarantee under normalization information: EF1 for n=2 and PROP1 for all n, improving on prior work whose algorithm can violate PROP1 even for n=2.

Theorem 5.1 gives a general and elegant meta-algorithm lifting any feasible offline share to the online setting with frequency predictions, yielding strong corollaries such as (3/4+3/3836)-MMS and EFX for n=2.

Strong impossibility results sharply delineate the limits of additional information: no positive EF1 approximation without information, no positive EFX with normalization, no positive EF1 for n>=3 with normalization, and no positive EFX for n>=3 with frequency predictions.
The identical-valuation section provides a tight bound: sqrt(5)-1/2-EFX is achievable for n=2 under normalization and identical valuations, and no online algorithm can do better.

Learning-augmented variants for noisy normalization and noisy frequency predictions show graceful degradation with explicit additive/multiplicative tradeoffs, and the limitations of additive EF1 robustness are carefully discussed.

The paper is honest about open problems and limitations, including the unresolved EF1 question for n>=3 with frequency predictions and the lack of a concrete instantiation rule with a standard prediction-error bound.
Proofs are detailed and mostly self-contained, and the algorithms are simple and polynomial-time whenever the underlying offline share can be computed in polynomial time.
weaknesses: Several proofs contain minor technical errors or typos that should be fixed: e.g., Theorem 4.3 has an off-by-one in the v2(g_{j+1}) value and an ambiguous expression '1-2^{-k^3+1}'; Theorem 4.4 lists v2(g2)=epsilon/3 in the second table but later uses epsilon/delta; and the V_i definition in Theorem 5.6 is ambiguous for n=3.

The learning-augmented frequency-prediction guarantee (Theorem 5.7) is parameterized by an internal instantiation error eta_i and does not provide a concrete instantiation rule whose error is bounded by a standard distance between predicted and true value multisets, making the robustness result somewhat tautological.
The frequency-prediction framework does not resolve EF1 for n>=3; this remains a significant open gap and limits the completeness of the information-model story.
Many impossibility results rely on relatively straightforward adversarial constructions, so the individual novelty of some results is modest, even though the overall collection is valuable.
The paper is dense and some notation (e.g., M_i, x_i, IDO profiles) and proof tables are hard to parse, which could hinder accessibility and reproducibility.

strengths: Comprehensive study of online fair division under multiple information models, covering no information, normalization, frequency predictions, and learning-augmented variants.

Strong impossibility results, including no positive EF1 approximation without information, no positive EFX approximation with normalization for n>=2, and no positive EFX approximation with frequency predictions for n>=3.
New algorithm for the normalization model that achieves PROP1 for any n and EF1 for n=2, with matching impossibilities that clarify what normalization information can and cannot buy.
General meta-algorithm for frequency predictions that lifts any feasible share-based offline guarantee to the online setting, matching the best-known offline MMS approximation.
Learning-augmented robustness guarantees for both noisy normalization and noisy frequency predictions, with explicit degradation in the error parameters.
Tight result for EFX under identical valuations and normalization for n=2, with a matching impossibility.
Proofs are generally rigorous and self-contained, and the paper honestly discusses limitations and open problems.
weaknesses: Several results are incremental adaptations of existing work: Algorithm 1 modifies Zhou et al.'s normalization algorithm, and multiple impossibility proofs follow known adversarial constructions.

The frequency prediction model is very strong (full multiset of future values per agent), and the meta-algorithm is essentially a simulation of an offline picking sequence, which may limit perceived novelty.
Presentation suffers from typos and notational inconsistencies that hinder verification, e.g., the table in Theorem 4.4 lists agent 2's g2 value as ε/3 while the proof uses ε/δ.

The learning-augmented guarantees are relatively straightforward perturbations of the exact-advice algorithms; the EF1 robustness under noisy normalization is only additive, which is weak although acknowledged.
The open problem of EF1 for n>=3 with frequency predictions remains unresolved, which is a significant gap given the strength of the advice model.

Randomized impossibility results rely on a very strong ex post pathwise guarantee under an adaptive adversary, limiting their practical relevance compared to weaker adversary or expectation-based models.

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic study of online fair division under several information models (no information, normalization, frequency predictions, identical valuations), clearly organized and summarized in Table 1.

Strong and tight impossibility results: no positive approximation for EF1 without information; no positive approximation for EFX with normalization even for n=2; no positive approximation for EF1 with normalization for n>=3; no positive approximation for EFX with frequency predictions for n>=3; and a tight phi-EFX bound for identical valuations with normalization for n=2.

Algorithm 1 for normalization information is a genuine improvement over prior work: it achieves EF1 for n=2 and PROP1 for any n, whereas the MMS rule of Zhou et al. (2023) can violate PROP1 even for two agents. The outside-good certificate idea is simple yet effective.

The meta-algorithm for frequency predictions (Theorem 5.1) is a significant conceptual contribution: it lifts any feasible offline share to the online setting, yielding the best-known (3/4 + 3/3836)-MMS guarantee online and EFX for n=2. The reduction via identically ordered (IDO) valuations and picking sequences is elegant and correct.

Learning-augmented variants for noisy normalization and noisy frequency predictions are well-motivated and provide graceful degradation. The additive EF1 and multiplicative kappa-PROP1 guarantees under noisy normalization are insightful, and the example showing multiplicative EF1 is impossible is a nice complement.
The extension of impossibility results to randomized algorithms under an adaptive adversary and ex post pathwise guarantees (Appendix A) is a clean observation, even if the model is strong.
The paper is theoretically rigorous overall; the main proofs are well-structured and the claims are supported by the technical arguments.
weaknesses: The presentation is very dense, with many results packed into a single paper. Some proofs are difficult to follow, and several minor typos or inconsistencies appear (e.g., in Theorem 4.4, v2(g2) is listed as ε/3 in the second table but the proof uses ε/δ, and the normalization sum does not match if the table is taken literally). Such issues could hinder verification and reproducibility.

The learning-augmented result for noisy frequency predictions depends on an unspecified online instantiation rule. The error parameter η_i is defined end-to-end, but no bounds are given in terms of standard prediction error metrics (e.g., Wasserstein distance) for the suggested instantiation rule, limiting practical guidance.

Some positive results are incremental modifications of prior work. For example, Algorithm 1 builds directly on the MMS algorithm of Zhou et al. (2023), and the impossibility without information for EF1 strengthens Benadè et al. (2018) using similar adversarial constructions.

The impossibility results for randomized algorithms assume a very strong ex post pathwise guarantee against an adaptive adversary. Many randomized online algorithms are analyzed in expectation or against oblivious adversaries, so these results do not fully rule out meaningful randomized fairness guarantees under more standard evaluation criteria.

The paper lacks experimental evaluation, which is acceptable for a theory paper but means there is no empirical validation of the learning-augmented components or the practical behavior of the algorithms.

The frequency prediction model assumes exact knowledge of the multiset of values for each agent and the total number of goods. While this is a standard semi-online model, the paper does not discuss how sensitive the guarantees are to misspecification of the number of goods or to errors in the multiset beyond the instantiation error.
